<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean A1/A2 compliance and sharp, evolving clash. B (PRO) won the decisive exchange: A's concession that low opt-in reflects "friction, not revulsion" because the data is worth "pennies" was flipped by B into the core case for the presumption — small, hidden, diffuse harm per person is exactly why opt-out regimes fail and an ex ante default is warranted ("a stranger may not lift a penny from every pocket"). B also answered both pressure questions directly (legible pay-or-walk price; ordinary regulatory scale lines) and defused A's "three statutes from the podium" charge by framing interpretation as application rather than amendment. A landed real hits — the proportionality argument against deploying law's strongest presumption for penny-value conduct, the blast-radius worry for small publishers, and the closing dilemma — but the dilemma was partially answered by B's "contextual and consented data fund content" plus "if not, nothing of value is lost," and A's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost. B's closing crystallized the vote ("who acts first, the taker or the taken-from?") more decisively than A's closing resolved the economic stakes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pivotal sequence was A4.1 accepting frictionless opt-in on the grounds that per-user value is "pennies," followed by B's Rebuttal 2 and Closing converting that very concession: B5.2–B5.3 argued that tiny, hidden, diffuse losses are precisely what individuals cannot litigate or opt out of, making rational ignorance the case for the presumption rather than against it — directly neutralizing A's strongest remaining economic argument and turning A's own framing into B's vote-winner.</best_rebuttal>
